'''''Knautia macedonica''''', the '''Macedonian scabious''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Caprifoliaceae]].<ref name=POWO>{{cite web |url= https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:319419-1 |title= Knautia macedonica Griseb. |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=n.d. |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=The Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=May 28, 2024}}</ref><ref name=COL>{{cite web |url= https://www.catalogueoflife.org/data/taxon/3R9XN |title= Knautia macedonica Griseb. |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=n.d. |website=Catalogue of Life |publisher=Species 2000 |access-date=May 28, 2024}}</ref> It is [[native species|native]] to Southeastern Europe: Albania, Bulgaria, Greece, North Macedonia, southeastern Romania  and [[Kırklareli]] in Turkey.<ref name = GRIN>{{GRIN}}</ref> Growing to {{convert|75|cm|in|abbr=on}}, this [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] produces rich red "pincushion" flowers, similar to those of its close relative scabious (''[[Scabiosa]]''), on slender upright stems throughout summer.<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/61000/Knautia-macedonica/Details | title = ''Knautia macedonica'' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref>

''Knautia macedonica'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]]. It is extremely hardy, down to {{convert|-20|C|F|abbr=on}} and below, but requires a sunny position in neutral or alkaline soil.<ref name = RHSPF/> Though it may be short-lived, it self-seeds readily.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.gardenia.net/plant/knautia-macedonica-macedonian-scabious | title = Knautia macedonica | website = Gardenia.net | publisher = Gardenia | access-date = 21 March 2021}}</ref>

==Description==

''Knautia macedonica'' is a [[flowering plant]] distinguished by its evenly distributed leaves along the stem, with the basal leaves typically withered by the time the plant flowers. The plant features undivided leaves, with the stem leaves ({{plantgloss|cauline}} leaves) having an {{plantgloss|ovate}}, {{plantgloss|crenate}}-{{plantgloss|serrate}} terminal lobe—meaning the leaf ends have an egg-shaped tip with rounded teeth along the edges.<ref name="Tubin 1976"/>

One of the most striking features of ''K. macedonica'' is its flower heads ({{plantgloss|capitula}}), which measure between 1.5 and 3 cm in diameter. The flowers typically display a deep, dark red colour, although [[lilac]] and pink variants can also occur. This colour variation is often found within the same population and may result from natural [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridization]] with related species such as ''[[Knautia arvensis]]'' and ''[[Knautia ambigua]]''. The plant has a [[chromosome]] count of 2''n''=20.<ref name="Tubin 1976"/>

''Knautia macedonica'' typically grows in scrubland and open woodland habitats. A biennial variant with broader-based stem leaves from southeastern Romania has been classified as ''[[Knautia tulceanensis]]''.<ref name="Tubin 1976"/>

==Habitat and Distribution==

''Knautia macedonica'' is native to the [[Balkan Peninsula]], where it naturally occurs in [[scrubland]] and open forest habitats. While indigenous to southeastern Europe, this ornamental plant has begun to expand its range through human cultivation and subsequent [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalization]].<ref name="Dudáš et al. 2023"/>

In Slovakia, ''K. macedonica'' has become a popular garden [[ornamental plant|ornamental]]. Observations have documented the first evidence of its spontaneous spread beyond cultivation in Slovak territory. The species was initially observed in village intravilans (built-up areas), suggesting that neighbouring private gardens served as the source of [[biological dispersal|dispersal]]. Research on the invasive potential of perennial plantations demonstrated the plant's capacity to spread readily into surrounding areas. These findings confirm the plant's ability to escape cultivation and establish itself in native habitats.<ref name="Dudáš et al. 2023"/> Similar patterns of naturalization have been observed in the Czech Republic, where ''K. macedonica'' was first recorded as a non-native species in 2018.<ref name="Lepší & Lepší 2019"/>
